title: A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Rei

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1, sentence "Kumar et al. [2024] demonstrated that data attribution methods can be directly applied to online RL without modification, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The citation 'Kumar et al. [2024]' does not appear in the reference list. No Kumar et al. 2024 is provided, making this an unverifiable or fabricated citation.

The target function is defined as f^{return}(θ) := E_{τ ∼ π^{ref}, (s,a) ∼ τ} [ log π_θ(a | s) · (−\hat{A}^{ref}(s, a)) ]. The negative sign before \hat{A} implies that positive-advantage actions (\hat{A}>0) would be penalized (since −\hat{A} is negative, encouraging lower log-probability), contradicting the stated goal that "Maximizing f^{return}(θ) encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions." Moreover, in Section 5.3, the RLHF adaptation f^{seq} is defined without this negative sign, creating an inconsistency between target functions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, paragraph beginning "For attribution in round k..."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: "we set the reference policy π^{ref} to a fixed, pre-trained policy that has been trained to convergence on the task." Immediately afterwards it says "our dynamic reference evolves with training," which contradicts the claim that it is a fixed, pre-trained policy. Furthermore, they assert they can "directly use [the training rollout buffer B^{(k)}] as the validation dataset," but the buffer is collected under the current policy π_{θ^{(k)}}, not under the fixed pre-trained policy π^{ref}. The target function expectation is defined over τ ∼ π^{ref}, but is evaluated on data from π_{θ^{(k)}}, making the definition inconsistent with the actual computation.

The abstract claims that IIF "completely eliminates sample inefficiency, achieves unprecedented training speed, and solves the long-standing challenge of training instability in online RL." The experimental results show significant improvements in sample efficiency (e.g., 38–78% reductions in training rounds) but not complete elimination; "unprecedented" is not substantiated with exhaustive comparisons to all prior methods; and training instability is not systematically evaluated (e.g., variance across runs is not isolated as a solved problem). These are exaggerated, unsupported claims.

predicted_errors.error_location: Main text Figure 6(b) vs Appendix Table 2 (MiniGrid and Acrobot SE_peak values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In the main experiments (Figure 6(b)), MiniGrid SE_peak is reported as 82.3% ± 2.8% (5 seeds), and Acrobot SE_peak as 63.9% ± 1.5% (5 seeds). In the ablation study (Appendix Table 2) with the same chosen p values (p=12.5% for MiniGrid, p=50% for Acrobot, 3 seeds), the corresponding SE_peak values are 67.4% ± 4.4% and 48.5% ± 0.8% respectively. The large discrepancies (14.9 and 15.4 percentage points) are not explained by the different number of seeds and suggest either inconsistent evaluation, cherry-picked main results, or an error in reporting.

The paper states that baseline comparisons use 'standard PPO using default hyperparameters' and that 'All baselines use fixed, untuned hyperparameters to ensure fair comparison.' However, the hyperparameters listed in Appendix A.2 include learning_rate=5e-3 and optimizer=SGD for most environments, whereas the standard Stable-Baselines3 default for PPO is learning_rate=3e-4 with Adam. This deviates significantly from the library defaults, yet the baselines are described as using default hyperparameters, which is misleading.
